question: An estate that gives the owner the greatest possible bundle of rights, with no limitation on duration or condition on continued ownership, is called:
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the highest form of ownership recognized in real property law, granting the owner unlimited duration and the full bundle of rights, subject only to governmental powers like taxation, police power, eminent domain, and escheat.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.a (freehold estate -- fee simple absolute), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A deed conveys land to a school district 'so long as the property is used for educational purposes.' If the district stops using it for a school, title automatically reverts to the grantor. This is a:
explanation: A fee simple determinable is created by durational language such as 'so long as,' 'while,' or 'during,' and automatically terminates -- reverting to the grantor -- the moment the stated condition is violated, without need for legal action.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.b (fee simple defeasible, determinable, condition subsequent), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An owner conveys property to their sister 'for the duration of her life,' after which it passes to a nephew. The sister's interest is a:
explanation: A life estate grants ownership and possession measured by a human lifetime; upon the life tenant's death, the property passes automatically to the remainderman (here, the nephew) named in the original conveyance.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.c (life estate), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A commercial tenant signs a lease running from January 1 through December 31 of the same year, with a fixed start and end date. This leasehold is an:
explanation: An estate for years has a definite, fixed beginning and ending date agreed to by the parties, and terminates automatically at the end date without requiring notice -- regardless of whether the term is actually a full year.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.3.a (estate for years and from period to period), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A tenant whose lease has expired remains in possession without the landlord's consent. This unauthorized holdover creates a(n):
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance arises when a tenant who lawfully entered the property continues to occupy it after the lease term ends without the landlord's permission, distinguishing it from trespass since the original entry was lawful.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.3.b (estate at will and estate at sufferance), Pearson VUE #094401

question: The recognized set of legal rights that accompanies ownership of real property -- including the rights to possess, use, encumber, sell, exclude others, and enjoy the property -- is commonly referred to as the:
explanation: The bundle of rights is the traditional conceptual framework describing ownership as a collection of separate, severable legal rights, any of which (such as mineral rights or an easement) can be sold, leased, or otherwise transferred independently of the others.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.A.2.d (bundle of rights), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Which type of deed offers the grantee the broadest protection, with the grantor warranting title against all defects, whether arising before or during the grantor's ownership?
explanation: A general warranty deed provides the strongest set of title covenants, with the grantor warranting against defects in title from the property's entire history -- not merely defects arising during the grantor's own period of ownership.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.2 (types of deeds), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A grantor conveys property using a deed that transfers only whatever interest the grantor currently holds, with no warranties of title at all. This is a:
explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys only the grantor's existing interest, if any, without any covenants or warranties -- commonly used to clear a cloud on title or resolve a boundary dispute rather than in typical arm's-length sales.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.2 (types of deeds), Pearson VUE #094401

question: When an owner dies leaving a valid will directing that real property pass to a named beneficiary, the transfer of title occurs through:
explanation: Transfer of title by will (devise) is a form of voluntary alienation because the deceased owner voluntarily directed the disposition of the property during their lifetime, distinguishing it from involuntary transfers like foreclosure or eminent domain.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.3.a (voluntary alienation), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A lender forecloses on a defaulted borrower and the property is sold at a trustee's sale. This transfer of the borrower's title is classified as:
explanation: Foreclosure transfers title without the owner's consent and is therefore a form of involuntary alienation, as are transfers through eminent domain, adverse possession, or a tax sale.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.3.b (involuntary alienation), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Recording a deed in the county clerk's real property records primarily serves to give:
choice_a: Actual notice only to the parties who signed the deed
choice_b: Automatic marketable title regardless of prior defects
choice_c: Constructive notice to the world of the recorded interest
choice_d: A guarantee against any future claims on the property
explanation: Recording provides constructive notice -- meaning the law presumes everyone is aware of a recorded instrument's contents, whether or not they actually looked it up -- which is why the recording system protects subsequent purchasers and creditors relying on the public record.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.4.a (constructive and actual notice), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A title search reveals an old, unreleased lien from a previous owner's paid-off loan still showing on the record. This defect that impairs marketability is called a:
explanation: A cloud on title is any recorded claim, lien, or encumbrance that appears to affect title validity, even if ultimately invalid or already satisfied; it must typically be resolved -- often through a quiet title action -- before title can be considered marketable.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.4.c (marketable title and cloud on title), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A policy that protects a buyer against covered title defects that existed before the buyer purchased the property, including defects not disclosed by the public record, is:
explanation: An owner's title policy insures the buyer/owner against covered title defects existing as of the policy date, including hidden defects like forged prior deeds or undisclosed heirs, which a title search might miss -- distinct from a lender's policy, which protects only the lender's security interest.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline II.B.4.d (attorney title opinion, quiet title lawsuit, title insurance), Pearson VUE #094401

question: In a Texas deed of trust financing arrangement, legal title is conveyed to a neutral trustee to hold as security for the lender until the loan is repaid. This reflects Texas's status as a:
choice_a: Pure lien theory state where the borrower always retains full legal title
choice_b: Title theory state that uses a deed of trust rather than a mortgage document as the standard security instrument
choice_c: State with no recognized security instruments for real estate loans
choice_d: State where only judicial foreclosure is permitted
explanation: Texas real estate financing is overwhelmingly structured through a deed of trust, a three-party instrument (borrower, lender, and trustee) that allows for the streamlined non-judicial foreclosure process used in the vast majority of Texas residential and commercial defaults.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline VII.A.2 (lien theory vs. title theory and deed of trust), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A buyer's interest in property purchased under a real property sales (land) contract, before legal title formally transfers at the end of the payment term, is known as:
explanation: Equitable title arises once a party has a contractual right to acquire legal title -- such as under a fully executed sales contract or contract for deed -- even though legal title itself has not yet passed at closing.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.3 (sales contract -- equitable title), Pearson VUE #094401
